svg.aria-label: Animated side-by-side comparison: LangGraph stock memory (checkpointer plus BaseStore and LangMem) versus langgraph-beads-memory (typed fact graph), run through the same three-conversation scenario. Phase A: a user states budget, self-host, and primary-source-only constraints; beads-memory captures the message and the turn's conclusion verbatim with no extraction LLM, while stock memory requires the agent to call manage_memory, which in the measured run it did not do (checkpointer history within the thread is genuinely complete, though). Phase B: a new thread_id resets message history in both; beads-memory recalls top-K facts across threads automatically, while stock memory requires the agent to call search_memory and finds nothing saved. Phase C: three sub-agents research pgvector, qdrant, and weaviate; beads-memory forks isolated hash-suffixed namespaces and enforces conclude_task with rollup_of edges back to raw exploration, synthesizing a fallback fact if a sub-agent crashes; stock memory returns sub-agent results as plain messages with no isolation and no audit edge, and a crashed sub-agent returns nothing, silently. Phase D, the sharpest contrast: a budget correction from $100k to $50k. beads-memory writes a typed supersedes edge that flips the old fact to superseded, retired from retrieval but kept for audit; stock memory would hold both values as separate documents with nothing marking which is current. Phase E, the real measured outcome, N=1, directional, not a benchmark: the treatment answered, quote, given the updated budget constraint of $50,000, Qdrant is the most suitable choice, end quote, while the baseline mentioned no budget figure and ended, quote, if you have any additional information or constraints, please let me know, end quote. Phase F is an honest scorecard: stock memory's real strengths are first-party simplicity, full history within a thread, real vector search in BaseStore, and verified cross-thread recall when the agent does save; at N=3 beads-memory used about 45 percent fewer input tokens, 10,083 versus 18,220, so its real cost is an extra dependency and Postgres schema rather than token overhead.

Within a thread, the checkpointer keeps full history — genuinely solid. Cross-thread continuity needs
the agent to call manage_memory; in run 0 it didn't.
A new thread_id means fresh message history. Continuity now depends on the agent choosing to
search_memory — and on something having been saved to find.
Sub-agent results return as messages into the parent's history. No enforced boundary between
siblings, and no edge from a conclusion back to the exploration that produced it.
A correction would become a second, separate document. Nothing marks which one is current —
similarity search can return either value.

svg.text: loop: capture → new thread → delegate → correction (supersedes) → outcome → scorecard · ~42s

g.text: Same session, three conversations, one correction — both memory designs, side by side.
Capture: beads-memory saves every user message and final answer automatically; stock memory needs
the agent to call manage_memory — it didn't, in run 0 (checkpointer history within-thread is solid).
New thread: beads-memory recalls top-K facts across thread_ids automatically; stock memory needs the
agent to call search_memory, and found nothing saved.
Delegation: beads-memory forks isolated namespaces with enforced conclude_task and rollup_of audit
edges, plus a crash fallback fact; stock memory returns results as plain messages with no isolation,
no audit edge, and a crashed sub-agent returns nothing, silently.
Correction ($100k → $50k): beads-memory flips a typed supersedes edge — old value retired, kept for
audit. Stock memory would hold both values with nothing marking which is current.
Measured: treatment answered "given the updated budget constraint of $50,000, Qdrant is the most
suitable choice." Baseline mentioned no budget figure at all.
Measured N=3: beads-memory used ~45% FEWER input tokens (10,083 vs 18,220). Its real cost is an extra
dependency and Postgres schema. See the scorecard panels below for the full breakdown.
